title: FAR Integrated Financial Statement Review
description: Combine recognition, measurement, presentation, disclosure, and financial statement effects across FAR.
html:
Think Across the Financial Statements

Many FAR questions are not really testing one isolated account.

They test whether you can follow an accounting event through the balance sheet, income statement, statement of cash flows, and equity.

TRANSACTION ↓ ACCOUNT BALANCES ↓ NET INCOME ↓ EQUITY ↓ CASH FLOW CLASSIFICATION

Scenario 1 — Accrued Expense

At year-end, a company has incurred $18,000 of salaries that have not yet been recorded or paid.

Salary Expense + $18,000
Salaries Payable + $18,000
Net Income − $18,000
Equity − $18,000

Because cash has not yet been paid, there is no immediate cash-flow effect from recording the accrual.

Scenario 2 — Accrued Revenue

A company has earned $25,000 of service revenue but has not yet billed the customer.

Receivable + $25,000
Revenue + $25,000
Net Income + $25,000
Equity + $25,000

Scenario 3 — Advance Customer Payment

A customer pays $48,000 in advance for 12 months of service.

Three months have been earned by year-end.

MONTHLY REVENUE = $48,000 ÷ 12 = $4,000 REVENUE EARNED = $4,000 × 3 = $12,000 CONTRACT LIABILITY = $48,000 − $12,000 = $36,000

Scenario 4 — Inventory Error

Ending inventory is overstated by $20,000.

ENDING INVENTORY OVERSTATED $20,000 ↓ COGS UNDERSTATED $20,000 ↓ NET INCOME OVERSTATED $20,000
Assets Overstated $20,000
COGS Understated $20,000
Net Income Overstated $20,000
Equity Overstated $20,000

Scenario 5 — Depreciation

Equipment has:

Cost: $260,000

Residual value: $20,000

Useful life: 8 years

ANNUAL DEPRECIATION = ($260,000 − $20,000) ÷ 8 = $30,000
Depreciation Expense + $30,000
Accumulated Depreciation + $30,000
Net Income − $30,000
Carrying Amount of Assets − $30,000

Depreciation and Cash Flow

Depreciation reduces net income but does not itself require a current-period cash payment.

Therefore, under the indirect method:

DEPRECIATION EXPENSE → ADD BACK TO NET INCOME IN OPERATING CASH FLOWS

Scenario 6 — Accounts Receivable Increase

Net income includes revenue that has not necessarily been collected in cash.

If accounts receivable increases by $15,000:

INDIRECT METHOD → SUBTRACT $15,000 FROM NET INCOME

Scenario 7 — Accounts Payable Increase

If accounts payable increases by $9,000, the company has generally recognized expenses that have not yet been paid in cash.

INDIRECT METHOD → ADD $9,000 TO NET INCOME

Working Capital Adjustment Pattern

OPERATING ASSET ↑ → SUBTRACT OPERATING ASSET ↓ → ADD OPERATING LIABILITY ↑ → ADD OPERATING LIABILITY ↓ → SUBTRACT

Scenario 8 — Sale of Equipment

Equipment has:

Cost: $150,000

Accumulated depreciation: $100,000

Cash proceeds: $62,000

CARRYING AMOUNT = $150,000 − $100,000 = $50,000 GAIN = $62,000 − $50,000 = $12,000

Sale of Equipment — Cash Flow Effect

CASH PROCEEDS $62,000 → INVESTING INFLOW

The $12,000 gain is included in net income, but under the indirect method it is removed from operating cash flow because the related cash proceeds belong in investing activities.

GAIN ON SALE → SUBTRACT FROM NET INCOME IN OPERATING SECTION

Scenario 9 — Bond Issuance

A corporation issues $500,000 of bonds for cash.

Cash Increase
Liabilities Increase
Net Income No Immediate Effect
Cash Flow Financing Inflow

Scenario 10 — Treasury Stock Purchase

A company pays $40,000 to reacquire its own common shares.

Cash − $40,000
Treasury Stock + $40,000
Total Equity − $40,000
Cash Flow Financing Outflow

Scenario 11 — Cash Dividend

When a cash dividend is declared:

RETAINED EARNINGS ↓ DIVIDENDS PAYABLE ↑

When the dividend is later paid:

CASH ↓ DIVIDENDS PAYABLE ↓ → FINANCING CASH OUTFLOW

Scenario 12 — Credit Loss Adjustment

Gross accounts receivable are $400,000.

The required ending allowance for credit losses is $24,000.

NET ACCOUNTS RECEIVABLE = $400,000 − $24,000 = $376,000

Increasing the allowance through credit-loss expense decreases net income and decreases the net carrying amount of receivables.

Scenario 13 — Loss Contingency

A lawsuit loss of $75,000 is probable and reasonably estimable.

Loss Expense + $75,000
Liability + $75,000
Net Income − $75,000
Cash No Immediate Effect

Scenario 14 — Unrealized Investment Gain

Be careful about where investment gains and losses are reported.

TRADING DEBT SECURITY → FAIR VALUE CHANGE → NET INCOME AVAILABLE-FOR-SALE DEBT SECURITY → UNREALIZED HOLDING GAIN OR LOSS → GENERALLY OCI

Net Income vs Comprehensive Income

COMPREHENSIVE INCOME = NET INCOME + OTHER COMPREHENSIVE INCOME

A transaction can affect comprehensive income without affecting current-period net income.

Integrated Adjustment Example

Assume preliminary net income is $300,000.

The following year-end adjustments have not yet been recorded:

Accrued salaries: $20,000

Accrued service revenue: $15,000

Depreciation expense: $25,000

Probable lawsuit loss: $10,000

Corrected Net Income

$300,000 − $20,000 + $15,000 − $25,000 − $10,000 = $260,000

FAR Integrated Strategy

FOR EVERY ADJUSTMENT: 1. IDENTIFY THE ACCOUNTS 2. DETERMINE WHETHER EACH ACCOUNT INCREASES OR DECREASES 3. DETERMINE THE NET-INCOME EFFECT 4. DETERMINE THE BALANCE-SHEET EFFECT 5. DETERMINE WHETHER CASH ACTUALLY MOVED 6. IF CASH MOVED, CLASSIFY THE CASH FLOW 7. RECHECK THE ACCOUNTING EQUATION

Cash Flow Classification Review

OPERATING → CORE BUSINESS CASH FLOWS INVESTING → LONG-LIVED ASSETS AND MANY INVESTMENTS FINANCING → DEBT AND EQUITY FINANCING ACTIVITIES

Common Exam Trap

Do not assume that an item affecting net income also belongs in operating cash flow for the same amount.

Gains and losses on investing activities are classic examples.

GAIN ON SALE OF EQUIPMENT → INCLUDED IN NET INCOME BUT CASH PROCEEDS ARE INVESTING

Another Common Trap

A noncash accounting adjustment can affect income and the balance sheet without changing cash at all.

ACCRUAL DEPRECIATION CREDIT-LOSS ESTIMATE CONTINGENCY ACCRUAL → MAY HAVE NO IMMEDIATE CASH EFFECT

Key Takeaways

  • Trace every FAR transaction through all affected financial statements.
  • Accrual accounting separates recognition from cash collection or payment.
  • Inventory errors affect both assets and income.
  • Depreciation reduces net income but is added back under the indirect cash-flow method.
  • Changes in operating assets and liabilities help reconcile net income to operating cash flow.
  • Gains and losses on asset disposals must be separated from the related investing cash proceeds.
  • Debt issuance and treasury-stock transactions are financing activities.
  • Some items affect OCI rather than current-period net income.
  • Noncash adjustments can change income and balance-sheet amounts without immediately changing cash.

quiz.prompt: A company reports preliminary net income of $300,000 before recording $20,000 of accrued salaries, $15,000 of accrued service revenue, $25,000 of depreciation expense, and a $10,000 probable and estimable lawsuit loss. What is corrected net income?
quiz.explanation: Start with $300,000. Accrued salaries reduce income by $20,000, accrued service revenue increases income by $15,000, depreciation reduces income by $25,000, and the lawsuit loss reduces income by $10,000. Therefore, corrected net income is $300,000 − $20,000 + $15,000 − $25,000 − $10,000 = $260,000.

objectives: Explain far integrated financial statement review and its underlying principles.
Apply the topic to a financial-reporting scenario.
Evaluate common errors and their financial-statement effects.
